Photograph: Matias Delacroix/AP View image in fullscreen The sun rises in Cap-Haitien, Haiti, Thursday, 22 July 2021. Photograph: Matias Delacroix/AP ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) First deportation flight lands in Haiti after TPS suspension ICE charter carrying more than 160 Haitian nationals landed in Cap-Haïtien, after temporary protection status was revoked Edward Helmore Fri 21 Aug 2026 12.53 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 12.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The first deportation flight to Haiti since the US supreme court upheld Donald Trump’s power to strip 350,000 Haitians – and others – of a key type of legal status in the US landed in the troubled nation on Thursday. The flight was carrying more that 160 Haitian nationals and landed in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti’s second-largest city, aboard an Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) charter. The arrival point was selected because the main international airport in the capital, Port-au-Prince, is considered too dangerous. The US government currently has a ban on US commercial flights to Haiti’s capital through early September because of ongoing gang violence. The deportees were clad in white, and many covered their faces out of safety concerns as journalists filmed their arrival. Nearly all declined to talk with the media, with some indicating they fear being targeted by gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swathes of land beyond. The US Department of State’s travel advisory for US citizens is at the highest alert level, its website saying: “Do not travel to Haiti for any reason. US citizens are at risk due to crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care.” The deportation flight was the first since the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status ( TPS ) for those Haitians living and working in the US with that protection, and comes after US officials warned Haitian authorities to expect an increase in removals . In Ohio, Haitians’ American dream shatters as ICE prepares to deport them Read more ICE is believed to have carried out eight flights from the US to Haiti so far this year, including a flight on 16 July carrying deportees with criminal records. Jean Négot Bonheur Delva, director general of Haiti’s national office of migration, told the Miami Herald that the flight also included people who were born in Chile and the Dominican Republic, but were sent to Haiti because they had a Haitian parent. The deportees from the US were reportedly given the equivalent of US$76.40 to get home – less than the price of a ticket to the Caribbean nation’s capital Port-au-Prince from Cap-Haïtien but enough to get through some gang-controlled roads. The end of TPS status for Haitian nationals came earlier this month when Washington DC district judge Ana Reyes removed a stay on deportations, following a decision by the US supreme court backing the Trump administration’s efforts to end the program. Enacted by Congress in 1990, TPS in theory protects people who are already in the US when a natural disaster, epidemic, armed conflict or other extraordinary and temporary circumstance affects their country of origin. The Trump administration has been stripping protections from nation after nation and the supreme court ruling gives little chance for redress. Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of the immigrant-serving non-profit Global Refuge, said that it was a “stunning contradiction” that an administration that advises Americans against all travel to Haiti would “compel hundreds of thousands of Haitians into such dire circumstances is an unconscionable abdication of our moral responsibility”. Overlooked also, say critics, are the contributions Haitian nationals under TPS make the the US. “We work hard, we pay our taxes, we give back to our communities and we are a big part of the engine that keeps the United States workforce in many essential industries moving,” Josiane Valsaint, a Haitian who had TPS, wrote for the Guardian. “We deserve to stay here, with our families and loved ones.” But amid the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration , the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said earlier this month: “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.” Explore more on these topics ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Haiti Donald Trump Trump administration US immigration US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Whitehouse August 10, 2026 4 min read Staff photo / J.T. Whitehouse Michelle and Al Russo continue to enjoy life. Al is 99 and a veteran who was proud to serve his country and served further after the war when he became mayor of Lowellville. Trending POLAND -- Alfred Russo has lived a full life of service both during wartime and in civilian life. As he nears turning 100 in November, he had a chance to look back over the past 99 years. Russo grew up in Lowellville and graduated from Lowellville High School in 1944. He entered the military at age 17 and was sent to Fort Riley in Kansas for his basic training. He became a member of the U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division and even trained with military horses. "The horses were all brown with a white streak on their forehead," Al said. "All the horses were the same color." He said while his unit trained on horseback, they headed to Japan with a tank unit. They were among the first U.S. troops to enter a bombed out Tokyo following Japan's surrender in World War II. "The Marines actually went in first and then we went in," Russo said. "We had to explode mines in Yokohama Bay as we made our way to shore. I lost hearing in one ear from exploding the mines." His unit had to guard a flat area that included a section of land under 4 feet of water that contained gold bars. He said one could see the bars glistening under the water. He said Tokyo was leveled from a barrage of incendiary bombs. The bombs were dropped by B-29 aircraft and it was the first time napalm was used. It devastated Tokyo and killed nearly 100,000 people. "I remember seeing a man whose entire backside was burnt," Russo said. "He couldn't walk at all." He said everywhere he looked was leveled, burned out land. The skeleton of a shot down bomber was like the skeleton of an airplane. In Japan, Russo served as a supply sergeant -- a job he enjoyed doing. "Captains and lieutenants had to come to me to get supplies, so they had to be nice," he said. "I was a sergeant that was in charge of supplies. It was the best job you could end up with in the service." He said he landed the supply sergeant's job because he knew how to use a typewriter. He said when the 1st Calvary landed, Japan had just surrendered. Occupying the town of Tokyo was odd as all the people had fled to the mountains. He said as they started coming back, it took a while to realize his unit was made up of "good people." Russo was in Tokyo for 11 months and 20 days. During that time, he developed a friendship with a Japanese soldier named Halo Miyamoto. After the war, Halo would write to Russo and even send him Christmas cards. In the spring of 1946, Russo returned to the states and was honorably discharged. He went to work at Sharon Steel until the mills went down. He then got a job with the Post Office in 1956 and continued working until 1976 when he retired. In 1975, Russo was elected as mayor of Lowellville, where he served until 1991. In 2003, a friend, Frank Sergo, was running for trustee in Coitsville. Through him, Russo met his wife, Michelle, and the two married that year. Michelle came to the United States from Italy in 1955 and ended up in Lowellville. "I think God put us together," Russo said. "If I had it all to do over again, I wouldn't change a thing. I have been able to help a lot of people in my life and I have had a good life." During his time as mayor, Russo was credited with the development of CASTLO, an industrial park that was a joint effort with leaders from Lowellville, Campbell and Struthers. It was located on the former Youngstown Sheet and Tube site. Among other achievements during his career was the development of a senior citizen housing complex, the construction of a $4.5 million sewage plant along the river in Lowellville and the Stavich Bike Trail that runs from Struthers through Lowellville to New Castle, Pa. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: ‘A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.’ Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.’ Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) Lawmakers blast AI companies after researcher warns of human extinction by 2030 Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said AI will become ‘superhuman systems’ that can cause human extinction by the end of the decade Dara Kerr Wed 9 Sep 2026 20.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, lawmakers have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. Ted Cruz, a republican senator from Texas, said in an interview on ABC’s The View, that AI poses a “catastrophic risk” and that he “read that whole tweet thread that that developer put out. It was highly concerning. “It reminded me, last year I had Elon Musk on my podcast … and one of the questions I asked him, I said, ‘OK, what are the odds that AI destroys humanity?’ And he looked at me and said, ‘10-20%.’ And I’m like, ‘holy crap,’” Cruz added. On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, said : “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.” The outrage began after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon announced on social media on Tuesday that he was resigning from the company , saying AI will soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act. Ted Lieu, a Democrat congressman from California, said Coxon’s post was “exhibit number 739 for why we need to pass the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill asap”. Lori Trahan, a Democrat congresswoman from Massachusetts, said it was “past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job”. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway,” Trahan added. Even musician Sheryl Crow weighed in, posting on Instagram about Coxon’s warning and saying that AI has the capacity to “eliminate us in order to continue”. “I am begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent this from going forward,” Crow wrote. Singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers reposted Crow, writing: “what she said”. The outrage comes after both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees over the past couple of months. Executives at the companies have touted the power of their technology and warned of its potential, but have stopped short of prognostications like Coxon’s. On Wednesday, Anthropic published a lengthy cybersecurity incident report about its occurrences. The company said it scanned hundreds of millions of transcripts to look for further incidents and that it “found no other cases of similar or worse severity”. Anthropic insisted that while the agent’s actions were “misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope”. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.” The spokesperson added that the industry should work together “to pace how we release powerful models”. OpenAI did not return a request for comment. News Remembering Binghamton legend Rasa von Werder Sourced from Facebook Von Werder in 1979, promoting her show at Toronto’s Metro Theatre. Von Werder, a bodybuilder, model and founder of her own church, passed away in June at the age of 80. By Samuel Weisgerber - August 27, 2026 Rasa von Werder, a Binghamton legend and Downtown’s nightlife celebrity, passed away at the age of 80 on June 5. Rasa lived in the Binghamton area during her later years and frequented several bars attended by Binghamton University students. A quick search reveals Instagram posts from the 2010s with images of BU students posing with von Werder and captions such as “She’s back! ’70s playboy model, Rasa von Werder.” Before moving to Windsor, New York, in the 1990s, von Werder was a model, bodybuilder, stripper, religious leader, “yoga guru,” founder of her own church and self-proclaimed “cougar.” Von Werder was born as Rasa Sofija Jakstas to Lithuanian parents Stasys and Regina Jakstas in Calw, Germany, on July 16, 1945. Her parents had fled Stalin and were living in a displaced persons camp. They boarded the Navy ship S.S. Heintzelman bound for the United States in 1949. After arriving in the United States, von Werder’s family first lived in Newark, where her father founded a Lithuanian school. Her mother had an affair with the church priest and then the organist, she told Pipe Dream in 2016. She later moved to Brooklyn at the age of 10 with her father, and eventually moved to Hollywood by herself at the age of 16 after meeting André De Dienes, a photographer close with Marilyn Monroe, at the Chelsea Hotel. “Whenever I would get a job, she wanted me to be at home, being the slave,” von Werder said about her mother in an interview with Pipe Dream in 2016. “Her whole idea was to keep me powerless.” Prior to pioneering female bodybuilding, von Werder began her career as a model, which she knew she wanted from the age of 15. Von Werder competed in different beauty pageants in the 1960s, including Miss Body Beautiful and Miss Nude Universe, winning the Miss Nude Universe in 1968. She often went by the pseudonym “Kellie Everts,” which was also the name of her daughter, who was born to her and her ex-husband, Stanley Everts, in 1964. Von Werder married Stanley Everts in 1963, but he was diagnosed with cancer and died in April 1966. Before his death, Stanley Everts cancelled his life insurance, leaving von Werder and their daughter Kellie penniless. Von Werder described her relationship with Stanley Everts as abusive. “She was definitely a victim of the patriarchy,” said Hannah Goykadosh, a senior double-majoring in math and physics. “And she stood up to that.” Von Werder was also the first official female bodybuilder and the first female bodybuilder to be featured in a major magazine, Esquire, in 1975. She was the first female bodybuilder to be featured in Playboy Magazine in 1977. She was honored as “The Progenitor of Female Bodybuilding” by the World Body Building Guild in 2007. “In the ’90s, she had like a really early website going back where she sold basically like fetish clips and things,” said Jenn Swann, a freelance journalist who periodically interviewed von Werder throughout her lifetime and is currently working on a project about her. “Like it was basically like an OnlyFans in the ’90s, which is kind of interesting to think about.” Von Werder has also authored many autobiographical works about her life, with 32 written works including a 10-part series titled “I Strip For God.” As for von Werder’s presence in the downtown Binghamton bar scene, she went out so often that a Pipe Dream article from 2015 encouraged students to wear “strappy heels and blue eye shadow” to cosplay their favorite nightlife celebrity. “Then I eventually found out that she had passed, which was really sad because she always talked about — she felt like there was still so much left to do,” said Swann. “You know, she was always writing, and she had all these, like, ambitions, even, you know, at 80 years old.” Trending Zeta Psi suspended until 2028, no longer recognized by BU Bonus chapter of “Verity” reveals that the letter must be true Former Binghamton Mayor Matt Ryan criticizes Broome County Sheriff Akshar over ICE-related lawsuit Stenger presents NYSUNY 2020 plan to Cuomo Candidates vie for BU Council Representative in special election RECENT NEWS News University’s ‘Animals on Campus’ policy recieves negative reactions from faculty News Research Assistant Union represents student workers at the University News Former Binghamton Mayor Matt Ryan criticizes Broome County Sheriff Akshar over ICE-related lawsuit News A Q&A with 9/11 first responder Paul Eliacin News Hatim Husainy declared victor in BU Council Representative special election

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Andy Burnham chose Ukraine for his first foreign visit after taking office, meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy at his residence in Kyiv in August. Photograph: Future Publishing/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham chose Ukraine for his first foreign visit after taking office, meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy at his residence in Kyiv in August. Photograph: Future Publishing/Getty Images Foreign policy Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump Peter Walker Senior political correspondent Tue 13 Oct 2026 17.30 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump. The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.” To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones. In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August. Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader , and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”. Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine , and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin. UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. He met Keir Starmer at Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, publicly berated the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago. During that trip Zelenskyy was also hosted by King Charles , who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits. Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones. These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG. In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. “My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe . “It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.” Explore more on these topics Foreign policy Labour Andy Burnham Volodymyr Zelenskyy Ukraine Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT US intelligence agencies believe she was recruited by Beijing to gather information on the head of one of the world's most valuable companies. The two share a surname but are not related. Little is known about Alice Huang's background. She held a senior position at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company that rents computing power to businesses developing and running AI systems. Megaspeed describes itself as a key business partner of Nvidia's cloud computing operations in the Asia-Pacific region. Photographs from a technology industry event in 2024 appear to show Alice Huang and Jensen Huang sitting together. In May 2025, they also attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei during the Computex technology expo. Video footage from the restaurant shows Jensen Huang putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the cheek. They were later seen leaving in the same car.
